description_full: Commerce Bancshares, Inc. operates as the bank holding company for Commerce Bank that provides retail, mortgage banking, corporate, investment, trust, and asset management products and services to individuals and businesses in the United States. It operates through three segments: Retail Banking, Commercial, and Wealth. The Retail Banking segment offers various banking products and services, including consumer deposits; consumer loans, such as automobile, motorcycle, marine, tractor/trailer, recreational vehicle, fixed rate and revolving home equity, and other consumer loans; patient health care financing; real estate loans; indirect and other consumer financing; retail branch network; personal mortgage banking; consumer installment lending; and consumer debit and credit bank cards. The Commercial segment provides corporate lending, leasing, international, merchant and commercial bank card, and securities safekeeping and bond accounting services; and business products, government deposits, and related commercial cash management services, as well as sells fixed income securities to correspondent banks, corporations, public institutions, municipalities, and individuals. The Wealth segment provides traditional trust and estate planning, advisory and discretionary investment portfolio management, and brokerage services, as well as private banking accounts. The company offers private equity investment, securities brokerage, insurance agency, specialty lending, and leasing services, as well as online and mobile banking services. Commerce Bancshares, Inc. was founded in 1865 and is headquartered in Kansas City, Missouri.

financial_summary: Commerce Bancshares, Inc. is a mid-cap financial services business with a $7.9B market cap on $1.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 17% against a 8% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $592M in free cash flow — roughly 34 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.14× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.5% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.3) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 12% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Trading at a 33% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
38 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 41% operating margin runs 12pp above the Financial Services median (29%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.60x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-1.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 514 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 8% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 7% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 9% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 18% and a beta of 0.66, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.13 vs 5y 0.61), so read it loosely.
About $53.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 14% in the 2022 bear market and 45% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 33% below its DCF fair value of $83.74, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 23%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $67.67 to $107 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-10%).
The 9 covering analysts target $64.06 on average, 15% above the price.
The price implies 2.2% annual cash-flow growth, 7pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 8.1% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.14).
It converts 34% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 15% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.8% over 3 years, 5.7% over 5 years and 5.0% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 5.0% on average.
Analysts expect 6.6% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.5%, and institutions hold 79%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $2.0M sold).
It returns 4.5% a year to shareholders (2.6% in buybacks and 2.0% in dividends).
The share count has grown 4.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 38 consecutive years, raising it 4.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 4,969 employees, each generates about $355K of revenue, 0.7x the Financial Services median, and revenue has grown 3.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $119K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.6M (10x revenue per employee).
